title: Operation Mincemeat
text:
In early 1943, after victory in North Africa, the Allies planned to invade Sicily. The target was so obvious that Winston Churchill reportedly said anyone but a fool would know it. British intelligence officers Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley developed an idea to make the Germans doubt it.

They obtained the body of Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who had died after swallowing rat poison, and turned him into a fictional officer, Major William Martin of the Royal Marines. They gave him a uniform, identity papers, and a carefully built private life: love letters and a photograph from a fiancee, a bank overdraft letter, theater ticket stubs. Chained to him was a briefcase holding personal letters between senior British generals that hinted, as if casually, that the Allies would land in Greece and Sardinia and only pretend to aim at Sicily.

On 30 April 1943 the submarine HMS Seraph released the body into the sea off Huelva, on the coast of neutral Spain, where a German agent was known to be active. The body washed ashore and was found by a fisherman. As the British hoped, Spanish officials allowed the Germans to see the documents, which reached Berlin and were judged genuine.

German forces were reinforced in Greece and Sardinia, among them a panzer division sent to Greece. When the Allies landed in Sicily on 10 July 1943, the defense was weaker than it would otherwise have been. The real identity of Major Martin was officially revealed only in 1996.
lesson: A convincing story is built from many small, ordinary details. People believe most readily what flatters their own judgment and seems to have been discovered by themselves.
people: Ewen Montagu, Charles Cholmondeley, Glyndwr Michael
source: Ewen Montagu, The Man Who Never Was (1953); Ben Macintyre, Operation Mincemeat (2010)
caveat: The exact military impact on the Sicily landings is debated by historians.
